opus-5.5.text:
Well, Geoff and I have known each other for a very long time. I was a postdoc in his lab in Toronto in the late eighties, so I have enormous respect for him, and we've remained friends even though we disagree on this quite strongly.

My understanding is that Geoff had an epiphany of sorts. He had been working on what he called biologically plausible learning algorithms, things like the forward-forward algorithm, trying to find something that could replace backprop and might be closer to what the brain does. At some point he concluded that backpropagation running on digital hardware might actually be *better* than what the brain does. Digital systems can share weights exactly, copy knowledge instantly across thousands of instances, and absorb far more data than any human. Then he saw what GPT-4 could do, and he thought, these systems may already understand quite a lot, they're going to get smarter than us, and we don't know how to control something smarter than us. That's when he left Google so he could speak freely about the risks.

I think the reasoning is sincere, but I disagree with the premise. I don't think autoregressive LLMs are anywhere close to human-level intelligence, or even cat-level intelligence. They manipulate language very fluently, and that fools us, because we associate fluency with intelligence. But they don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan in any deep sense. A four-year-old child has seen more data through vision than the largest LLM has seen through text. So we're missing something essential, and I've been arguing that we need new architectures, world models, things like JEPA, objective-driven systems, to get there.

And on the risk side, I don't buy the idea that intelligence automatically comes with a desire to dominate. That's a human trait, a product of evolution for social species. We can design AI systems with objectives and guardrails that make them controllable and subservient to us. It'll be an engineering problem, like making turbojets safe, not some existential mystery.

So I'd say Geoff is a brilliant scientist who changed his mind based on what he observed, which is to his credit. I just think he drew the wrong conclusion. The systems we have today are impressive, useful, but they're not the precursor to a superintelligence that's going to take over. We're still missing the key ingredients.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, Geoff is a friend. We've known each other for almost forty years. I did my postdoc with him in Toronto in 1987. So I say this with a lot of affection: I think he's wrong on this one.

What happened is that GPT-4 came out, and Geoff was surprised by how well it performed. Really surprised. And I think his conclusion from that surprise was, "If I underestimated how fast this would go, then maybe the whole trajectory is faster than I thought, and maybe the scary scenarios are closer than I thought." And then he left Google so he could speak freely about it, and he's been very vocal since.

Now, I was less surprised, frankly, because I'd been looking at these systems and their limitations pretty closely. Auto-regressive LLMs are impressive. They have absorbed an enormous amount of human text. But they are fundamentally limited. They don't understand the physical world. They don't have persistent memory. They can't really reason in the sense of planning a sequence of actions to achieve a goal. They predict the next token. And producing fluent text is something that fools people, because for humans, fluent language has always been correlated with intelligence. For these systems, it isn't.

So where Geoff and I diverge is on two things. The first is whether scaling these systems gets you to human-level intelligence. I think it does not. We're going to need new architectures, systems that learn world models from observation, like a baby does, like a cat does. A cat has a better model of the physical world than any LLM. The second is the question of danger. Geoff worries about systems developing their own goals, wanting to take over, and so on. I think that's a projection of human nature onto machines. Intelligence does not imply a desire to dominate. That desire is a product of evolution in social species. We're going to build these things, and we're going to build them with objectives and guardrails, and if a design is dangerous we won't deploy it. Just like we do with jet engines.

And frankly, the political consequence of Geoff's position worries me. If you say AI is an existential risk, the natural conclusion is to lock it up, regulate research, keep it in the hands of a few companies. I think that's much more dangerous than the technology itself. The future should be open-source, with a diversity of systems from all over the world, not a handful of proprietary models controlling what everyone knows.

So, we argue about it. We've argued about it on stage, on social media. He thinks I'm being complacent. I think he's extrapolating from a surprise. But we're still friends, and I think that's the way science should work.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that GPT-4 caused Geoff to revise his view of how much intelligence you can get from large language models. He became much more convinced that these systems could surpass human intelligence sooner than he had expected, and much more concerned about what would happen then. I don’t want to speak for him about his personal reasons, but that’s how I understand the change.

I disagree with the conclusion. To me, being very good at manipulating language is not the same as understanding the world. These systems still have significant limitations in reasoning, planning, and understanding physical reality. So there are two separate questions: Will we eventually build systems that are smarter than humans? I think yes. Does that mean they will inevitably seek power or escape our control? I don’t think that follows. Intelligence does not automatically come with a desire to dominate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Geoff and I look at the same results and draw different conclusions. A system like GPT-4 can make you update very strongly on how much intelligence you can get from predicting the next word. But there are several separate questions here: How capable is the system? Does it understand the world? And does greater capability imply that it will become dangerous or want to take control?

You can be impressed by the first without accepting all the others. My disagreement is with treating those steps as inevitable. Being intelligent and having a desire to dominate are not the same thing. You have to explain where the objectives come from, how the system is designed, and what constraints it operates under.

So I take Geoff’s concerns seriously. But the fact that these systems surprised us is a reason to study them carefully, not, by itself, evidence for a particular catastrophic scenario.
